cards.title: Neurons and networks
cards.hook: A neuron fires when a weighted combination of its inputs passes a threshold.
cards.visual:
ActivationFormulaRange / use
Step1 if x ≥ 0 else 0{0, 1}, perceptron
Sigmoid1/(1 + e^(−z))(0, 1), probability output
Tanh(e^{2x} − 1)/(e^{2x} + 1)(−1, 1), centred
ReLUmax(0, x)[0, ∞), efficient hidden layers

example: Inputs (1, 2), weights (0.5, −1), bias 0.5: in = 0.5 + 0.5 − 2 = −1 → ReLU 0, sigmoid 0.269.
cards.trap: There is no single best activation: choose by problem, layer type and training behaviour.
explain: An artificial neuron is a tiny calculator inspired by brain cells: it multiplies each input by a weight (how much it cares about that input), adds them up together with a bias, then passes the total through an activation function.
Neurons are arranged in layers: an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. Each link carries one weight; learning means adjusting these weights.
The activation adds non-linearity. Without it, stacking layers would still only give a straight-line (linear) model. ReLU is the usual choice for hidden layers; sigmoid suits probability outputs.

tex.t: in_j = \sum_{i} w_{i,j}\, a_i \;(+\, w_{0,j}), \qquad a_j = g(in_j)
where: weight on the link i → j

cards.title: Perceptron and its learning rule
cards.hook: Nudge the weights toward the right answer only when the perceptron is wrong.
cards.visual:
Casey − hWeight change
Correct0none
Missed a positive (y=1, h=0)+1w += αx
False positive (y=0, h=1)−1w −= αx
cards.memory: Wrong → move toward the example (or away).
cards.trap: The bias input x₀ = 1 also gets updated.
explain: A perceptron is a single neuron with a hard on/off output: if the weighted sum is at least 0 it outputs 1, otherwise 0. It draws a straight line that separates two classes.
The bias w₀ (weight on a constant input of 1) slides that line or threshold left or right.
Learning rule: if the prediction is right, change nothing. If it is wrong, nudge every weight toward the correct answer by α × error × input.

tex.t: ws = \sum_{j=0}^{n} w_j x_j \;(x_0 = 1), \qquad h_w(\mathbf x) = \begin{cases}1 & ws \ge 0\\ 0 & ws < 0\end{cases}

cards.title: Gradient descent and backpropagation
cards.hook: Errors flow backward, layer by layer, to tell every weight how to change.
cards.visual:
QuantityFormula
Output errorΔ₅ = 2(ŷ − y)g′(in₅)
Hidden errorΔ₃ = Δ₅ w₃,₅ g′(in₃)
Gradient∂L/∂w₃,₅ = a₃Δ₅; ∂L/∂w₁,₃ = x₁Δ₃
Updatew ← w − α·aᵢΔⱼ
formula: non-linear layer + linear layer ≈ any continuous function
cards.memory: Gradient = what comes in × error going out.
cards.trap: Vanishing gradient: error signals are extinguished as they propagate back through many sigmoid layers.
explain: Training a network = gradient descent on its loss. The difficulty is finding how each hidden weight affects the final error.

Backpropagation solves this with the chain rule: compute the error signal Δ at the output, then pass it backwards. Each hidden unit's Δ is the Δ of the units it feeds, times the connecting weight, times its own activation slope g′.
The gradient for any weight is simply (activation coming in) × (Δ at the receiving unit). With sigmoid, g′ = g(1 − g) ≤ 0.25, so signals shrink layer by layer: the vanishing-gradient problem.

tex.t: \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{i,j}} = a_i\,\Delta_j, \qquad w_{i,j} \leftarrow w_{i,j} - \alpha\, a_i\,\Delta_j

cards.title: RNNs and LSTMs (Workshop 5)
cards.hook: An LSTM adds a protected memory lane so information survives many steps.
cards.visual:
GateDecides
Forget fₜkeep (≈1) or reset (≈0) each memory element
Input iₜwhich new information to ADD
Output oₜhow much memory to expose as zₜ
formula: Markov assumption on the hidden state
example: 'I grew up in Sydney … therefore I speak English': a plain RNN may forget 'Sydney'; an LSTM can keep it.
cards.memory: Forget, Input, Output: F-I-O, like a fridge (throw out, put in, take out).
cards.trap: LSTM gradients don't vanish as fast because new information is ADDED, not repeatedly multiplied.
explain: A recurrent network feeds its own hidden state back in at the next time step, so it carries memory of earlier inputs.
Backpropagating through many time steps multiplies by w_zz (and g′ ≤ 1) again and again: values below 1 make gradients vanish, above 1 make them explode.

An LSTM adds a memory cell cₜ that is copied forward and updated by ADDING new information. Three gates (numbers between 0 and 1) control it: forget (keep or wipe), input (how much new info to add), output (how much to reveal as zₜ).

tex.t: z_t = g_z(W_{zz} z_{t-1} + W_{xz} x_t), \qquad \hat y_t = g_y(W_{zy} z_t)
f_t = \sigma(W_{xf}x_t + W_{zf}z_{t-1}),\; i_t = \sigma(W_{xi}x_t + W_{zi}z_{t-1}),\; o_t = \sigma(W_{xo}x_t + W_{zo}z_{t-1})
c_t = c_{t-1}\odot f_t + i_t \odot \tanh(W_{xc}x_t + W_{zc}z_{t-1}), \qquad z_t = \tanh(c_t)\odot o_t
